Measurements of similar systems in the firn of both Greenland and Antarctica indicate the maximum lateral development and contour of such a pool to be one of circular configuration with a diameter of approximately 60-m (Reed and Tobiasson, 1968). Such a technique imposes neither health nor hygiene risks for camp personnel and creates no long- or short-term impacts on the contiguous environment. When the project is completed and the camp abandoned, this site will be marked with bamboo poles and signs. The subsurface pool will gradually freeze. A conservative estimate of the time required for total freeze-back is about one year after abandonment. Since the ice shelf in this vicinity moves seaward, this frozen material will ultimately appear at the ice front and calve as an iceberg to the open ocean. At the estimated rate of movement this might require 1,000 years. The subsequent melting of the berg will be a gradual process, so the resulting deposition of the waste materials will not exert an adverse effect on the ocean environment.
9. Monitoring Scientific Use of Radioisotopes. The only anticipated use of radioactive isotopes is for the study of the productivity levels beneath the Ross Ice Shelf. Less than 1-m Ci of C-14, dissolved as sodium carbonate in a liquid and contained in glass ampoule will be required for this purpose. The material will be transported following ERDA regulation and will be logged in with the Radiation Safety Officer at McMurdo. The material will be used in closed glass containers and after use will be placed in special containers to convert the material to a biologically inactive substance. This waste will be returned to McMurdo for disposal
